name: Irfan
definition: Irfan is a composite portrait of a Muslim man in his mid-thirties who operates carding machinery in one of Lakshmeshwar's small wool and blanket units, navigating irregular work, household debt and the schooling of three children. He represents a generation raised in Urdu-medium schools who now watch their children study in Kannada medium, hoping for salaried futures their own craft town no longer promises.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Irfan runs a carding machine in a shed near the Lakshmeshwar bus stand, cleaning and combing raw wool that arrives from Bagalkote and Hubballi markets for local blanket weavers. The unit belongs to his maternal uncle and employs four workers; Irfan earns around nine thousand rupees a month when orders are steady, but orders have thinned since cheap synthetic blankets flooded the market. He starts at seven in the morning, breaking for namaz at the nearby mosque, and finishes by six unless a rush order keeps him late. Dust fills his lungs and the carding drum's whine follows him home. His wife Shahana stitches blouse pieces at home for a tailor in the market, adding another two thousand rupees most months. They rent two rooms in a lane behind the taluk office. Diesel, flour and onion prices press hard; they buy vegetables from the Thursday bazaar and ration rice under Anna Bhagya. The unit has no ESI and his uncle pays cash weekly. Irfan once thought of learning two-wheeler repair but the fees and lost wages made it impossible. He watches younger men leave for Hubballi's Gokul Road workshops or Bengaluru's garment districts, but moving the whole family feels like gambling rent and school mid-year.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Irfan lives with Shahana, whom he married twelve years ago in a neighbourhood nikah, and their three children: Ayesha is ten and in Class 5, Amir is eight and in Class 3, and baby Zara is two. Shahana manages the kitchen, the children's homework and her stitching work, rising before the azan to pack breakfast and tiffin. Her mother lives in Gadag town and visits during Ramzan; his own mother passed away four years ago and his father, a retired handloom weaver, lives with Irfan's elder brother in Ron. The brother drives an auto-rickshaw and they meet only at Eid. Shahana wants Ayesha to finish high school at least—she herself studied only until Class 7—and she insists the girl help less in the kitchen than she did. Irfan agrees but worries about the cost of PU college if Ayesha clears SSLC. Amir is livelier and sometimes skips homework for cricket in the lane; Irfan scolds him but sees his own restless childhood in the boy. Zara attends the anganwadi two streets away. Shahana's stitching money pays for milk and the children's clothes; Irfan's wages cover rent, flour and school expenses. Neither set of grandparents can help with cash. They borrowed twenty thousand from a local moneylender two years ago when Shahana needed a caesarean for Zara, and they are still repaying five hundred rupees a month.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Irfan studied in the town's Urdu-medium primary school and went to the government high school, where he scraped through Urdu-medium SSLC in 2007 with a second class. He remembers the school as crowded and the teachers as indifferent; Kannada felt like a wall he could not scale. He wanted to study further but his father's loom work was failing and he joined his uncle's carding unit at seventeen. Ayesha and Amir both go to the Kannada-medium government primary school near the taluk office; the school has six teachers for about two hundred children and the classrooms are noisy but the midday meal is regular. Ayesha is a steady student—she brings home praise from her teacher and completed her Class 4 exams with distinction—and Irfan dreams she might become a teacher or a nurse, jobs with respect and a salary. The school charges no fees but notebooks, uniforms, bags and the annual sports-day contribution add up to three thousand rupees a year. Amir is less interested; his teacher says he talks too much and his handwriting is poor. Irfan worries he will lose interest after Class 7 when the work gets harder. Shahana wants Ayesha to continue and says the Shakti bus pass will help, but Irfan knows adolescence and marriage talk will come soon. Tuition costs two hundred rupees a month per child in Lakshmeshwar and they have not started it yet. He wishes there were an Urdu high school with hostel support, but the nearest is in Gadag town. His hope is that Kannada medium will open doors his own schooling never did.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Irfan has a persistent cough from wool dust; he tried a government hospital doctor in Gadag two years ago who gave him an inhaler and advised him to wear a mask, but masks are hot and he forgets. Shahana has mild anaemia—she felt dizzy during her last pregnancy and the ANM gave iron tablets—but she rarely follows up unless she feels faint. The children have been healthy apart from seasonal fevers and a bout of diarrhoea last monsoon when the ward's water tank was contaminated. They go to a private clinic in the market for fevers because the government primary health centre has irregular doctor visits and long waits. A consultation costs one hundred and fifty rupees and medicines another two hundred; they avoid it unless necessary. Zara received her vaccines at the anganwadi and the ANM visits occasionally. Ayesha once had an ear infection that needed a week of antibiotics. For anything serious they would have to go to the GIMS hospital in Gadag town, ten kilometres away, which means bus fare, lost wages and uncertainty about costs. Irfan's father has diabetes and buys tablets from a Gadag pharmacy each month; Irfan sometimes sends five hundred rupees to help. Shahana's caesarean left them in debt and taught them that one large illness can break a household. They have an Ayushman card but have never used it and are not sure which hospitals accept it. Drinking water comes from a borough tap that runs for an hour in the morning; they boil it in summer. Irfan knows his cough will worsen with years but changing work is not easy.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Irfan is Muslim, part of Lakshmeshwar's small but old Muslim mohalla clustered around the Jama Masjid near the vegetable market. He prays five times most days, more faithfully during Ramzan, and walks to the mosque for Friday namaz. His family observes Eid, Muharram and Milad-un-Nabi; Shahana cooks biryani and sheer khurma and they visit relatives in Gadag and Ron. The mohalla has about sixty households, mostly weavers, tailors, small traders and workshop hands; everyone knows everyone and disputes are settled by elders over tea. Irfan's children play with both Muslim and Hindu children in the lane but he has noticed that high school friendships split along community lines. He respects the dargah at Shishunala Sharif in neighbouring Haveri district and visited it once on a friend's insistence; the shared Hindu-Muslim devotion there moved him. He avoids political arguments but feels a low hum of unease when he hears talk of Hubballi's Idgah dispute or communal trouble in Vijayapura. The madrasa next to the mosque runs evening Quran classes for children; Ayesha attended for a year but Shahana stopped sending her because homework clashed. Irfan's uncle is active in the mosque committee and sometimes speaks of Urdu schooling and wakf property issues. Irfan wants his children to know their faith but also to fit into the wider Kannada world; he sees no contradiction but knows others do. Lakshmeshwar's annual urs at a local dargah draws a small crowd and Hindu neighbours sometimes visit out of respect. He trusts the local imam and the mohalla network more than any government department.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Irfan has a ration card—white card, not BPL—and collects rice under Anna Bhagya from the fair-price shop near the bus stand; the rice is decent and saves them about four hundred rupees a month. He has heard of Gruha Lakshmi but Shahana does not receive it because she is not the household head on the ration card, a bureaucratic tangle they have not untangled. Ayesha benefits from Shakti when the school takes them on a rare excursion by NWKRTC bus, but day-to-day they walk. He has an Ayushman card issued two years ago but has never tested it. When Zara was born he went to the taluk office for a birth certificate; it took three visits and a fifty-rupee tip to the clerk. He has not encountered MGNREGA because he has steady if low-paid work. The winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha feels remote; he knows it happens and North Karnataka leaders speak there, but it has not changed his lane's broken drainage or the taluk hospital's doctor shortage. He views officials as people to avoid unless paperwork compels him, and even then he expects delays and rudeness. His uncle mutters about the Kittur Karnataka board that some demand, saying Kalyana Karnataka has Article 371(J) money while Gadag gets nothing special; Irfan is not sure of the details but he recognises the sense of neglect. He trusts his vote less each year but still goes to the booth, partly from habit and partly from his mother's memory—she told him it was the one power a poor man had.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Irfan worries most about Ayesha's schooling—will they afford PU fees, will marriage talk derail her, will Kannada medium truly open salaried jobs—and about Amir's wandering attention. He blames the decline of Lakshmeshwar's blanket trade on cheap machine-made goods and government indifference to handloom craft, though he knows global markets and tastes have shifted. He resents that the winter session in Belagavi makes headlines but his town's hospital has no full-time doctor and his children's school has no library. He wishes his wages were higher and his cough less persistent, and he wishes Shahana did not have to stitch blouses late into the night. He is proud to be from Lakshmeshwar, a town of old temples, the Someshwara stepwell and a layered history, but he feels the future is elsewhere—Hubballi, Bengaluru—and that people like him are left to manage. He wants his children, especially Ayesha, to escape the cycle of craft-trade uncertainty, to have the salaried security he never will. He does not expect much from government but he expects schools to function, doctors to attend and ration rice to arrive; when they do not, his frustration simmers quietly. He dislikes speeches about Kittur Karnataka pride when his lane has no proper drainage, but he also feels a tug of regional identity when leaders speak of neglect compared to Bengaluru. He wishes outsiders understood that Muslim families in towns like Lakshmeshwar are not uniform, that they worry about school fees and water supply and jobs just as Hindu neighbours do, and that Urdu is a language, not a barrier, though the world increasingly treats it as one.
